# Why Generative Bayesian Computation? {#sec-introduction}

> "*All models are wrong, but some are useful.*" -- George Box

Bayesian statistics provides a coherent framework for learning from data under uncertainty. You specify a prior $\pi(\theta)$ and a likelihood $p(y \mid \theta)$, and Bayes' theorem delivers the posterior $\pi(\theta \mid y)$ --- the complete answer to any inference question. This much is settled. The open question is *computation*: how do we actually get our hands on the posterior?

For the past four decades, the dominant answer has been Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC). You construct a Markov chain whose stationary distribution is the posterior, run it for a very long time, and hope that the samples you collect are representative. This strategy works, and it has transformed applied statistics. The development of MCMC methods --- from the Metropolis algorithm in 1953 through the Gibbs sampler in the 1980s to Hamiltonian Monte Carlo and the No-U-Turn Sampler that power modern probabilistic programming languages --- is one of the great success stories of computational statistics.

But MCMC comes with a cost: convergence diagnostics, mixing failures in high dimensions, and the need to rerun the chain from scratch for every new dataset. These are not minor inconveniences --- they are fundamental bottlenecks that limit the scale and speed of Bayesian analysis. In a world where models are growing more complex, datasets are growing larger, and inference must happen in real time, these bottlenecks become increasingly binding.

This book develops an alternative. **Generative Bayesian Computation (GBC)** replaces MCMC with a neural network trained by stochastic gradient descent. The idea is simple: simulate a large collection of (parameter, data) pairs from the prior and likelihood, then train an implicit quantile network (IQN) to learn the map from data to posterior quantiles. Once trained, the network produces posterior samples for *any* observed dataset via a single forward pass --- no chains, no burn-in, no convergence diagnostics. The posterior quantile function is the fundamental object: it encodes everything we need to know about the posterior distribution, and it can be learned from simulated data using standard supervised learning techniques.

Consider a concrete example that will recur throughout this book. NASA's Langley Glide-Back Booster (LGBB) is a reusable rocket concept whose aerodynamic drag coefficient depends on three input variables: Mach number (the speed of the vehicle relative to the speed of sound), angle of attack (the angle between the velocity vector and the vehicle's longitudinal axis), and sideslip angle (the angle between the velocity vector and the vehicle's plane of symmetry). These three inputs together determine the aerodynamic forces on the vehicle, and understanding how drag depends on them is critical for trajectory optimization and mission planning.

Engineers run a computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulator to predict the drag coefficient at any combination of these inputs. The simulator solves the Navier-Stokes equations on a fine mesh around the vehicle geometry, and each simulation takes hours on a high-performance computing cluster. A complete characterization of the drag surface would require tens of thousands of simulations --- far too many to run at full fidelity. The inferential question is: given a limited budget of CFD runs and noisy wind-tunnel measurements, what can we learn about the drag surface? Can we build a fast surrogate that predicts drag accurately at untested flight conditions?

MCMC fails here because the CFD simulator is a black box --- there is no closed-form likelihood to evaluate, only a forward code that maps inputs to outputs. You cannot compute $p(\text{drag} \mid \text{Mach}, \text{angle})$ as a function; you can only run the simulator and observe the output. ABC can in principle handle this, but the summary statistics needed to capture the three-dimensional drag surface are themselves high-dimensional, and the acceptance rate collapses as the dimension of the summary grows.

GBC takes a different route. The approach is to simulate thousands of (input, drag) pairs from the prior distribution over inputs and the CFD simulator, building up a dataset of $N$ pairs $\{(x_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^N$ where $x_i = (\text{Mach}_i, \text{angle}_i, \text{sideslip}_i)$ and $y_i = \text{drag}_i$. We then train an IQN on these pairs. The IQN learns the conditional quantile function $Q_{y|x}(\tau)$, which gives the $\tau$th quantile of the drag coefficient conditional on the input parameters. For any new set of wind-tunnel observations, we can produce posterior quantiles over the input parameters in milliseconds via a single forward pass through the trained network.

The trained network learns the entire relationship between inputs and outputs across the full design space, so it generalizes to flight conditions that were not in the original training set. This amortization property is what makes GBC practical for engineering workflows where the same model must be queried repeatedly under different conditions, for instance during trajectory optimization where the drag surface must be evaluated at thousands of candidate flight profiles.

The LGBB example also illustrates the role of *active learning* in GBC. Because each CFD simulation is expensive --- hours of compute time on a cluster for a single (Mach, angle, sideslip) configuration --- we want to choose the input configurations intelligently rather than using a space-filling design. GBC's ensemble uncertainty estimates --- obtained by training multiple IQNs with different random initializations and comparing their predictions at test points --- identify regions of the input space where the model is most uncertain. These are typically regions near the boundaries of the flight envelope, where the drag surface changes rapidly and the training data are sparse. By sequentially adding simulations in these uncertain regions, we can achieve high accuracy with far fewer total simulations than a passive design would require.

We develop this example fully in @sec-active-learning, where GBC with active learning achieves an RMSE of 0.00723 on the LGBB benchmark, a factor of $2.95\times$ better than deep Gaussian processes. The LGBB problem will serve as a running example in several chapters: we introduce the data in @sec-datasets, build a basic surrogate in @sec-surrogates, and develop the active learning strategy in @sec-active-learning.

The theoretical foundation is the **noise outsourcing theorem** [@kallenberg1997foundations], which guarantees that any conditional distribution $Y \mid X$ can be represented as $Y = G^*(U, X)$ where $U \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)$ is independent of $X$ and $G^*$ is a deterministic measurable function. The function $G^*(\tau, x) = Q_{Y|X}(\tau \mid x)$ is the conditional quantile function --- the object we learn. This theorem tells us that the representation we seek exists and is a well-defined mathematical object.

The computational engine is the **Implicit Quantile Network** (IQN), borrowed from distributional reinforcement learning and repurposed for statistical inference. The IQN takes the quantile level $\tau \in (0,1)$ and the input $x$ (or data summary $z$) and produces the conditional quantile $\hat{Q}(\tau \mid x)$. It is trained using the pinball loss on simulated data, and it can represent arbitrary conditional distributions --- not just Gaussian, not just symmetric, not just unimodal.

This chapter frames the entire book. We begin by comparing three paradigms for Bayesian computation --- MCMC, ABC, and GBC --- on the same simple problem, so that the reader can see concretely what each approach computes and at what cost (@sec-intro-paradigms). We then define GBC precisely and preview how it works, emphasizing the four-step algorithm and the properties that distinguish it from existing methods (@sec-intro-what-is-gbc). A brief look at the IQN architecture (@sec-intro-iqn-preview) introduces the computational engine that powers all applications. We describe the five application domains where GBC excels --- surrogates, inference, prediction, decision-making, and causal inference --- with enough detail to convey the scientific motivation for each (@sec-intro-five-applications). We position our approach relative to classical Bayesian computation, mapping every standard method to its GBC counterpart (@sec-intro-vs-classical). We trace the intellectual lineage that led to GBC, from Parzen's quantile philosophy through Rubin's simulation principle to the IQN architecture borrowed from distributional RL (@sec-intro-history). Finally, we lay out the road map for the rest of the book with forward references to specific results (@sec-intro-roadmap).


## Three Paradigms for Bayesian Computation {#sec-intro-paradigms}

There are three main strategies for turning the abstract formula
$$
\pi(\theta \mid y) \propto p(y \mid \theta) \, \pi(\theta)
$$ {#eq-intro-bayes}
into a usable computational object. Each makes a different trade-off between generality, accuracy, and computational cost. We describe each in turn, then work through a concrete example --- the normal-normal conjugate model --- to see all three in action on the same problem. 
The three paradigms can be understood through a simple analogy. Imagine you want to learn the shape of a mountain you have never seen. MCMC is like sending a hiker who walks around the mountain following a specific set of rules (the Metropolis algorithm), recording the altitude at each step. After a long hike, the trail of recorded altitudes approximates the mountain's shape. ABC is like asking many people to describe mountains they have seen, and keeping only the descriptions that match photographs of your target mountain. GBC is like training an artist to draw any mountain given a photograph, by showing the artist thousands of (photograph, mountain) pairs. Once trained, the artist can sketch your mountain from a single photograph. Each approach works, but the computational economics are very different.

*MCMC: The Workhorse.*

Markov chain Monte Carlo constructs a Markov chain $\theta^{(1)}, \theta^{(2)}, \ldots$ whose stationary distribution is the posterior $\pi(\theta \mid y)$. The chain is designed so that, regardless of the starting point, the distribution of $\theta^{(t)}$ converges to $\pi(\theta \mid y)$ as $t \to \infty$. After a sufficient burn-in period (discarding the initial transient samples), the remaining samples approximate the posterior, and expectations can be estimated by sample averages: $E[g(\theta) \mid y] \approx T^{-1} \sum_{t=1}^T g(\theta^{(t)})$.

The Metropolis algorithm [@metropolis1953equation], its generalization by @hastings1970monte, the Gibbs sampler [@geman1984stochastic; @gelfand1990sampling], and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo [@neal2011mcmc] with the No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS) [@hoffman2014no] that powers Stan [@carpenter2017stan]. NUTS in particular deserves mention: by automatically tuning the step size and number of leapfrog steps, it made HMC practical for a wide range of models without user intervention. Standard textbook treatments [e.g., @gelman2013bayesian; @robert2004monte] provide comprehensive coverage of these methods, and probabilistic programming languages --- Stan, PyMC, NumPyro, Turing.jl --- have made MCMC accessible to practitioners across the sciences, from ecology to epidemiology to astrophysics.

But MCMC has structural limitations that become increasingly apparent as problems grow in scale and complexity.

First, there is no general-purpose criterion that guarantees a chain has converged. We run multiple chains, compute $\hat{R}$ statistics, and inspect trace plots --- all heuristic. The split-$\hat{R}$ diagnostic of @vehtari2021rank is the current state of the art, but even it provides only a necessary condition for convergence, not a sufficient one. A chain can pass all diagnostics and still have failed to explore the full posterior.

Second, posterior geometry becomes treacherous as dimension grows. Multimodal posteriors require the chain to jump between modes, which happens exponentially rarely for random-walk proposals. Funnel geometries --- common in hierarchical models --- cause the chain to get stuck in the narrow end. Near-singular covariances in high-dimensional posteriors lead to slow exploration. These are not hypothetical concerns; they arise routinely in applied Bayesian work.

Third, each observed dataset requires a fresh MCMC run. Fitting the same model to 10,000 sensors means 10,000 separate chains, each costing $O(Tn)$ where $T$ is the chain length and $n$ is the sample size. There is no way to reuse the work done for one dataset when analyzing the next.

Finally, at every iteration MCMC must evaluate the likelihood $p(y \mid \theta)$. For simulator-based models --- agent-based models, climate simulators, cosmological codes --- the likelihood has no closed form, and standard MCMC simply does not apply. The model can generate data given parameters, but it cannot evaluate the probability of observed data given parameters. This is the situation GBC was designed for.

*ABC: The First Likelihood-Free Method.*

Approximate Bayesian Computation (ABC) was the first systematic attempt to perform Bayesian inference without evaluating the likelihood. The idea, due to @rubin1984bayesianly, is that Bayesian inference can be recast as a pure simulation exercise: draw $\theta$ from the prior, simulate $y^{\text{sim}}$ from the model, and accept $\theta$ whenever $y^{\text{sim}}$ is "close" to the observed data $y_{\text{obs}}$. If the simulator is a faithful representation of reality, then parameters that produce data similar to what we observed are the ones that are plausible given the data --- which is exactly what the posterior captures.

In its simplest form (rejection ABC), one draws $\theta$ from the prior, simulates $y^{\text{sim}} \mid \theta$, and accepts $\theta$ if $y^{\text{sim}} = y_{\text{obs}}$. For continuous data this acceptance probability is zero, so in practice one compares low-dimensional summary statistics $S(y^{\text{sim}})$ and $S(y_{\text{obs}})$, accepting when $\|S(y^{\text{sim}}) - S(y_{\text{obs}})\| < \varepsilon$ for some tolerance $\varepsilon > 0$. The resulting samples approximate $\pi(\theta \mid S(y_{\text{obs}}))$ --- the posterior conditioned on the summary statistic, not the full data. More sophisticated variants --- MCMC-ABC, sequential Monte Carlo ABC (SMC-ABC), and regression-adjusted ABC --- improve efficiency but share the same fundamental structure. The method was formalized for population genetics by @tavare1997inferring and @beaumont2002approximate, and has since been applied across biology, ecology, and the physical sciences [@marin2012approximate].

ABC can be understood as a *kernel density estimator* of the posterior. The acceptance region $\|S(y) - S(y_{\text{obs}})\| < \varepsilon$ defines a local kernel centered at the observed summary. This interpretation, developed by @blum2013comparative, reveals both ABC's strength (no likelihood needed) and its weakness (the curse of dimensionality). As the dimension of $S$ grows, the volume of the acceptance region shrinks exponentially, and the acceptance rate collapses. As $\varepsilon \to 0$, the approximation improves (converging to the exact posterior projected onto $S$) but the computational cost explodes. The practical consequence is that ABC works well when the summary statistic is low-dimensional (say $k \leq 5$) but becomes impractical when $k$ is large.

There is also the question of *which* summary statistic to use. If $S$ is not sufficient for $\theta$, then ABC targets $\pi(\theta \mid S(y_{\text{obs}}))$, not $\pi(\theta \mid y_{\text{obs}})$, and information is lost. Choosing good summary statistics is an art, and the ABC literature has devoted considerable effort to it [@fearnhead2012constructing]. GBC faces the same challenge but handles it differently: the summary statistic can be learned as part of the training procedure, using a neural network to approximate the posterior mean $E[\theta \mid y]$, which is an approximately sufficient statistic by Kolmogorov's theorem.

*GBC: From Kernels to Neural Networks.*

Generative Bayesian Computation replaces ABC's local kernel with a global neural network. Both methods share the same first step --- simulate $(\theta_i, y_i)$ pairs from the prior and likelihood --- but they differ fundamentally in how they use the simulated data.

*ABC* uses the simulations locally: for each new observed dataset $y_{\text{obs}}$, it finds the simulated pairs whose summary statistics are close to $S(y_{\text{obs}})$ and uses them as approximate posterior samples. This is kernel smoothing: each new query requires scanning the entire simulated database, and the quality depends on how many simulations happen to fall near the observed summary.

*GBC* uses the simulations globally: it trains a neural network on *all* simulated pairs to learn the conditional quantile function $Q_{\theta \mid S}(\tau \mid s)$ over the entire summary-statistic space. Training happens once. At inference time, the network is evaluated at $S(y_{\text{obs}})$ --- a single forward pass, regardless of how many simulated pairs exist.

This distinction has concrete consequences. ABC suffers the curse of dimensionality in the summary statistic space because kernel estimators do [@schmidt-hieber2020nonparametric]. In $k$ dimensions, a kernel estimator requires $O(\varepsilon^{-k})$ samples to achieve tolerance $\varepsilon$, which becomes prohibitive for $k > 5$ or so. With 10 summary statistics, even a generous tolerance of $\varepsilon = 0.1$ yields an acceptance rate of roughly $0.1^{10} = 10^{-10}$, requiring $10^{10}$ simulations to get a single posterior sample.

GBC breaks this curse when the underlying function has compositional structure, because deep ReLU networks exploit hierarchy that flat kernels cannot. The result, due to @schmidt-hieber2020nonparametric, is that the minimax rate for a deep ReLU network approximating a compositional function $f = g_L \circ \cdots \circ g_1$ depends on the *effective* dimension at each layer, not the ambient dimension of the input. If each component function $g_l$ maps from $d_l$ dimensions to $d_{l+1}$ dimensions, the rate depends on $\max_l d_l$, not on the input dimension $d_0$. This is the theoretical basis for GBC's scalability, and we develop it rigorously in @sec-proofs.

The reader familiar with modern Bayesian computation might wonder: what about variational inference? Variational methods [@blei2017variational] approximate the posterior by optimizing over a family of tractable distributions $q(\theta)$, minimizing the KL divergence $\text{KL}(q \| \pi(\cdot \mid y))$. They are fast and scalable, and they have been enormously successful in machine learning --- variational autoencoders, for instance, use variational inference as a core component.

We do not include variational inference as a fourth paradigm because GBC subsumes its main advantages while avoiding its principal limitations. Variational inference requires evaluating the likelihood (or at least its gradient with respect to parameters) at every optimization step, just as MCMC does. The evidence lower bound (ELBO) that variational methods optimize contains the expected log-likelihood as a term, and computing this term requires pointwise likelihood evaluation. For simulator-based models, this is a non-starter.

Variational inference also introduces a structural approximation error: the posterior is constrained to lie in the variational family (typically a factorized Gaussian), which may miss important features like multimodality, heavy tails, or complex correlation structure. Mean-field variational Bayes, the most common choice, assumes independence across parameter blocks, which can badly underestimate posterior variance.

GBC, by contrast, does not evaluate the likelihood, and the quantile function representation is nonparametric --- it can represent any continuous distribution, not just members of a specified parametric family. Where variational inference approximates $\pi(\theta \mid y)$ with a tractable distribution, GBC approximates the quantile function $Q_{\theta \mid y}(\tau)$ with a neural network, and the approximation error is controlled by the network's capacity, not by the expressiveness of a parametric family. Normalizing flows [@rezende2015variational] address some of variational inference's expressiveness limitations by using invertible neural networks, but they still require likelihood evaluation. GBC requires only simulation.

To make this concrete, let us work through the simplest possible Bayesian problem --- the normal-normal conjugate model --- and see all three paradigms side by side.

### A Mini-Example: Normal-Normal Inference {#sec-intro-normal-normal}

Suppose we observe $n$ data points $y_1, \ldots, y_n$ from a normal model with unknown mean $\theta$ and known variance $\sigma^2 = 1$:
$$
y_i \mid \theta \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} N(\theta, 1), \quad i = 1, \ldots, n.
$$
We place a conjugate normal prior $\theta \sim N(\mu_0, \sigma_0^2)$ with $\mu_0 = 0$ and $\sigma_0^2 = 1$. This is the simplest nontrivial Bayesian model, and it is one of the few where we can work out the answer by hand. We use it here as a calibration device: since we know the correct posterior analytically, we can verify that GBC recovers it. The strategy of testing on problems with known answers before trusting the method on problems without known answers is a recurring theme in this book.

We now apply all three paradigms to this same problem.

*Analytic Solution.* The posterior is available in closed form. The prior precision is $1/\sigma_0^2 = 1$ and the data precision is $n/\sigma^2 = n$. The posterior precision is their sum, $n + 1$, and the posterior mean is the precision-weighted average of the prior mean and the data mean:
$$
\theta \mid y_{1:n} \sim N\!\left(\frac{n \bar{y}}{n + 1}, \; \frac{1}{n + 1}\right),
$$ {#eq-intro-conjugate}
where $\bar{y} = n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n y_i$ is the sample mean. The posterior mean is a weighted average of the prior mean $\mu_0 = 0$ and the data mean $\bar{y}$, with weights proportional to their respective precisions. The posterior variance $1/(n+1)$ shrinks as $n$ grows, reflecting increasing certainty about $\theta$. For instance, if $n = 10$ and $\bar{y} = 2.3$, the posterior mean is $10 \times 2.3 / 11 = 2.09$, the posterior standard deviation is $1/\sqrt{11} = 0.302$, and the 95% credible interval is approximately $[2.09 - 1.96 \times 0.302, \; 2.09 + 1.96 \times 0.302] = [1.50, \, 2.68]$.

*MCMC (Metropolis--Hastings).* Even though we know the answer, let us pretend we do not and run a Metropolis--Hastings random walk. At each iteration $t$, we propose a new value $\theta'$ by adding Gaussian noise to the current value:
$$
\theta' = \theta^{(t)} + \epsilon, \quad \epsilon \sim N(0, \delta^2),
$$
for some step size $\delta$ (often called the proposal scale). We then compute the acceptance probability
$$
\alpha = \min\!\left(1, \; \frac{p(y \mid \theta') \, \pi(\theta')}{p(y \mid \theta^{(t)}) \, \pi(\theta^{(t)})}\right),
$$
and set $\theta^{(t+1)} = \theta'$ with probability $\alpha$, otherwise $\theta^{(t+1)} = \theta^{(t)}$. After discarding a burn-in of, say, 1,000 iterations and thinning every 10th sample from a chain of length 10,000, we get approximately 900 effectively independent posterior samples. The trace plot should look like white noise centered near 2.09, the autocorrelation should decay quickly, and $\hat{R}$ should be close to 1.0 if we run multiple chains.

This works well for a one-dimensional problem. But notice two things.

First, the choice of $\delta$ matters: too small and the chain takes tiny steps, auto-correlating heavily and exploring the posterior slowly; too large and most proposals are rejected, and the chain rarely moves. Finding a good $\delta$ requires tuning, typically targeting an acceptance rate around 23--44% depending on dimension. For our one-dimensional normal model, the optimal acceptance rate is about 44%, and $\delta \approx 2.4 \times \sigma_{\text{post}} = 2.4/\sqrt{11} \approx 0.72$ works well. But in higher dimensions, tuning becomes harder, and the optimal $\delta$ shrinks, causing the chain to explore more slowly.

Second, at every single iteration we had to evaluate the likelihood $p(y \mid \theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n \phi(y_i - \theta)$. For our normal model this is cheap --- a few floating-point operations. But for a climate simulator or a CFD code, each "likelihood evaluation" is a full simulation that might take hours. For an agent-based model, there may not even be a way to evaluate the likelihood; you can simulate forward but not compute probabilities backward. That likelihood-evaluation requirement is precisely what GBC eliminates.

*GBC (Implicit Quantile Network).* We proceed differently, in three stages. First, we generate the training data by simulation. For each $i = 1, \ldots, N$ with $N = 100{,}000$, draw a parameter value $\theta_i \sim N(0, 1)$ from the prior, then draw data $y_{i,1}, \ldots, y_{i,n} \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} N(\theta_i, 1)$ from the likelihood, and compute the summary statistic $z_i = \bar{y}_i = n^{-1} \sum_{j=1}^n y_{i,j}$. This gives us $N$ training pairs $\{(\theta_i, z_i)\}_{i=1}^N$. Note that we have simulated from the model --- drawing $\theta$ and then $y \mid \theta$ --- but we have never *evaluated* the likelihood as a function. We only used it as a simulator.

Second, we train an IQN $G_\phi(\tau, z)$ on these pairs using the pinball loss. During each training iteration, we sample a batch of pairs $\{(\theta_i, z_i)\}$ and, for each pair, draw a random quantile level $\tau_i \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)$. The loss for each pair is $\rho_{\tau_i}(\theta_i - G_\phi(\tau_i, z_i))$, where $\rho_\tau$ is the pinball loss. We minimize the average loss over the batch using the Adam optimizer. Over many epochs, the network learns to map any summary statistic $z$ and any quantile level $\tau$ to the corresponding posterior quantile. Training takes a few minutes on a laptop for this simple problem.

Third, for the observed data with $\bar{y}_{\text{obs}} = 2.3$, we produce posterior samples by drawing $\tau_1, \ldots, \tau_B \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)$ and returning $\{G_\phi(\tau_b, 2.3)\}_{b=1}^B$. The resulting posterior quantiles match the analytic solution --- the median is near $2.09$, the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles near $1.50$ and $2.68$ --- but the computation is a single forward pass through a trained network, taking under 0.05 seconds.

More importantly, the *same trained network* works for any other observed $\bar{y}$: plug in $\bar{y} = 0.5$ or $\bar{y} = -1.7$ and get the corresponding posterior instantly. MCMC would require rerunning the entire chain from scratch for each new dataset. This is what we mean by *amortized inference*: the cost of training is paid once, and then inference for any number of future datasets is essentially free. For a sensor network with 10,000 sensors, each producing a dataset with the same model structure, GBC trains once and then produces 10,000 posteriors in under a second of total computation. MCMC would need 10,000 separate chains.

The normal-normal example is deliberately simple --- it is one where MCMC works perfectly and GBC offers no practical advantage. The point is methodological: all three paradigms give the same answer, confirming that GBC targets the correct posterior. The advantages of GBC emerge when we move to problems where the likelihood has no closed form, where amortization over many datasets matters, or where the posterior has complex structure that challenges MCMC mixing. We encounter all of these situations in later chapters.

It is also worth comparing what each method *returns*. MCMC gives a collection of correlated posterior samples --- typically thousands of $\theta$ values that approximate the posterior but exhibit serial dependence because they come from a Markov chain. The effective sample size (ESS) is usually much smaller than the nominal number of samples. ABC gives a collection of approximate posterior samples (approximate because of the $\varepsilon$-tolerance) that are independent but target a smoothed version of the posterior.

GBC gives something quite different: the posterior *quantile function* $G_\phi(\tau, z)$ as a learned object --- a function you can evaluate at any $\tau \in (0,1)$ for any summary statistic $z$. This is a *functional representation* of the posterior, not a finite collection of samples. From the quantile function, you can produce independent samples (draw $\tau$ uniformly and evaluate $G_\phi$), compute any quantile directly (evaluate at the desired $\tau$), compute credible intervals (evaluate at $\tau = \alpha/2$ and $\tau = 1 - \alpha/2$), compute the posterior CDF at any point $t$ (find $\tau$ such that $G_\phi(\tau, z) = t$), and compute posterior expectations via numerical integration: $E[g(\theta) \mid z] = \int_0^1 g(G_\phi(\tau, z)) \, d\tau$. The quantile function is a richer object than a bag of samples, and this richness is exploited throughout the book, particularly in the decision-theoretic applications of @sec-meu where expected utility can be computed as a simple one-dimensional integral over $\tau$.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" title="The \"No MCMC\" Thesis"}
GBC produces the *same Bayesian answers* as MCMC --- posterior quantiles, credible intervals, point estimates, predictive distributions --- but via a fundamentally different computation. There are no Markov chains, no convergence diagnostics, and no burn-in. There is no likelihood evaluation at test time. The approach is amortized: train once, then query for any observed dataset in milliseconds. And it scales linearly in sample size, at cost $O(NLw^2)$ where $N$ is the number of simulated pairs, $L$ is the network depth, and $w$ is the width.

GBC is not anti-Bayesian. It is a different *computational strategy* for the same inferential target.
:::

@tbl-intro-paradigms summarizes the three paradigms.

| | *MCMC* | *ABC* | *GBC (IQN)* |
|---|---|---|---|
| *What it computes* | Posterior samples via chain | Posterior samples via rejection | Posterior quantiles via neural net |
| *Training cost* | $O(Tn)$ per dataset | $O(N/\varepsilon^k)$ per dataset | $O(NLw^2)$ once |
| *Inference cost* | Rerun chain | Rerun rejection | Forward pass ($\sim$0.05s) |
| *Amortized* | No | No | Yes |
| *Likelihood needed* | Yes (evaluated at each step) | No (simulation only) | No (simulation only) |
| *Density-free* | No | No | Yes |
| *Max sample size* | $\sim 10^4$ | $\sim 10^3$ | $90{,}000+$ |
| *Convergence* | Diagnostics required | $\varepsilon$-tolerance | SGD (standard training) |

: Comparison of three paradigms for Bayesian computation. The training cost for MCMC and ABC is per dataset; for GBC it is a one-time cost. {#tbl-intro-paradigms}



## What is Generative Bayesian Computation? {#sec-intro-what-is-gbc}

GBC turns Bayesian inference into a supervised learning problem. If we can simulate from the joint distribution of parameters and data --- that is, draw $\theta \sim \pi(\theta)$ and $y \mid \theta \sim p(y \mid \theta)$ --- then we have access to training data for the conditional distribution $\theta \mid y$, which is exactly the posterior. The noise outsourcing theorem (developed fully in @sec-noise-outsourcing) guarantees that this conditional distribution can be represented as a deterministic function of a uniform random variable and the data: $\theta = G^*(\tau, S(y))$ where $\tau \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)$ and $G^*$ is the conditional quantile function. Learning $G^*$ from the simulated pairs is a standard regression problem --- we just need the right loss function (the pinball loss) and the right architecture (the IQN).

The algorithm has four steps.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" title="Algorithm 1.1: Generative Bayesian Computation"}
*Input:* Prior $\pi(\theta)$, simulator $p(y \mid \theta)$, summary statistic $S(\cdot)$.

1. *Simulate.* Draw $\theta_i \sim \pi(\theta)$ and $y_i \sim p(y \mid \theta_i)$ for $i = 1, \ldots, N$.

2. *Compute features.* Set $z_i = S(y_i)$. If sufficient statistics are unknown, learn $S$ via a neural network [@jiang2017learning].

3. *Train IQN.* Learn $G_\phi(\tau, z) \approx Q_{\theta \mid z}(\tau)$ by minimizing the pinball loss over the simulated pairs $\{(\theta_i, z_i)\}_{i=1}^N$.

4. *Inference.* For observed data $y_{\text{obs}}$, compute $z_{\text{obs}} = S(y_{\text{obs}})$, draw $\tau_1, \ldots, \tau_B \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \text{Uniform}(0,1)$, and return posterior samples $\{G_\phi(\tau_b, z_{\text{obs}})\}_{b=1}^B$.
:::

In Step 1, GBC generates $(\theta_i, y_i)$ pairs by forward simulation from the prior and likelihood --- the same step that ABC uses. The key difference is that GBC uses *all* simulated pairs for training, whereas ABC discards most of them (keeping only those close to the observed data). This difference is enormous in practice. If we simulate $N = 500{,}000$ pairs and the ABC acceptance rate is $0.1\%$, then ABC retains only 500 samples while GBC trains on all 500,000. The full dataset provides a much richer training signal for learning the posterior quantile function.

In Step 2, the summary statistic $S$ plays the same role as in ABC: it reduces the dimensionality of the data from $n$ (the number of observations) to some lower dimension $k$. When sufficient statistics are known (as for exponential family models), we use them. For a normal model, $S(y) = (\bar{y}, s^2)$ suffices; for a Poisson model, $S(y) = \sum y_i$ suffices. When sufficient statistics are not known --- which is the typical situation for simulator-based models --- @jiang2017learning showed that training a neural network to predict $\theta$ from $y$ (i.e., approximating the posterior mean $E[\theta \mid y]$) produces an approximately sufficient statistic. The posterior mean is a function of the sufficient statistic (by the sufficiency principle), so learning it effectively performs data compression without discarding information about $\theta$.

Step 3 is where GBC departs most radically from both MCMC and ABC: it turns posterior estimation into a regression problem. The training data are the simulated pairs $\{(\theta_i, z_i)\}$, augmented with random quantile levels $\{\tau_i\}$ drawn uniformly from $(0,1)$. The regression target is $\theta_i$, the regressor is $(z_i, \tau_i)$, and the loss function is the pinball loss $\rho_{\tau_i}(\theta_i - G_\phi(\tau_i, z_i))$. This is a standard supervised learning problem that can be solved by stochastic gradient descent using any modern deep learning framework.

Step 4 is the payoff: inference for any new dataset is a single forward pass through the trained network, costing milliseconds regardless of the model's complexity. You compute the summary $z_{\text{obs}} = S(y_{\text{obs}})$, draw $\tau$ values uniformly, and evaluate $G_\phi(\tau, z_{\text{obs}})$.

*Density-free.* GBC never evaluates the likelihood $p(y \mid \theta)$. We only need to *simulate* from it. This is strictly weaker than knowing the likelihood in closed form, and it is the reason GBC applies to simulator-based models where MCMC fails. Consider several examples. An agent-based model of disease spread: given a transmission rate $\theta$, we can simulate 10,000 epidemics and record the outcomes, but we cannot write down $p(y \mid \theta)$ as a function because the epidemic dynamics involve stochastic interactions among millions of agents. A cosmological simulation: given cosmological parameters (dark matter density, dark energy equation of state, etc.), we can simulate the evolution of the universe and predict the cosmic microwave background power spectrum, but the likelihood mapping parameters to observations involves solving coupled partial differential equations. In both cases, MCMC is blocked because it needs to evaluate the likelihood at every iteration; GBC proceeds because it needs only to simulate from the model.

*Amortized.* Steps 1--3 happen once, offline. Step 4 is a forward pass through a trained network --- it takes roughly 0.05 seconds regardless of the complexity of the model. If you need posteriors for 10,000 datasets, you run 10,000 forward passes, not 10,000 MCMC chains.

This amortization property transforms the economics of Bayesian inference. The cost is dominated by the one-time training, not the per-query inference. For problems where the same model is queried repeatedly --- sensor networks monitoring air quality across a city, astronomical surveys cataloguing millions of galaxies, genomic studies analyzing thousands of patient samples --- the savings are dramatic. The training cost is fixed (say, 2 hours on a GPU), and then each query costs 0.05 seconds. For 10,000 queries, the total time is $2 \text{ hours} + 10{,}000 \times 0.05 \text{ s} \approx 2 \text{ hours and } 8 \text{ minutes}$. With MCMC at 30 seconds per chain, the same analysis would take $10{,}000 \times 30 \text{ s} \approx 83 \text{ hours}$.

*Quantile-based.* The output is the posterior quantile function, not a density. Quantile functions are more fundamental than densities --- every distribution has a quantile function, but not every distribution has a density. A discrete distribution, a mixture of a continuous distribution and a point mass, a distribution with atoms --- none of these have densities in the classical sense, but all have perfectly well-defined quantile functions.

And quantile functions give you everything you need for practical inference. The posterior median is $G_\phi(0.5, z_{\text{obs}})$. A 95% credible interval is $[G_\phi(0.025, z_{\text{obs}}), \; G_\phi(0.975, z_{\text{obs}})]$. Posterior samples come from evaluating $G_\phi$ at uniform random $\tau$ values. The posterior mean is $\int_0^1 G_\phi(\tau, z_{\text{obs}}) \, d\tau$, computable by quadrature. The posterior variance is $\int_0^1 [G_\phi(\tau, z_{\text{obs}}) - \bar{G}]^2 \, d\tau$ where $\bar{G}$ is the mean. And expected utility, as we show in @sec-meu, is a one-dimensional integral of the form $\int_0^1 U(G_\phi(\tau, z_{\text{obs}})) \, d\tau$. The quantile function is a complete representation of the distribution, and it is the representation that GBC computes naturally.

*Theoretical guarantee.* The noise outsourcing theorem [@kallenberg1997foundations] guarantees that the map $G^*(\tau, z) = Q_{\theta \mid z}(\tau)$ exists for any joint distribution $(\theta, z)$ in a Borel space. This is not an approximation theorem --- it is an existence theorem. The conditional quantile function $G^*$ is well-defined, measurable, and uniquely determined (up to sets of measure zero). The universal approximation theorem for deep ReLU networks [@hornik1989multilayer; @schmidt-hieber2020nonparametric] then guarantees that a sufficiently large network $G_\phi$ can approximate $G^*$ to arbitrary precision.

The combination means GBC is not a heuristic --- it is a principled approximation to an exact Bayesian object. The approximation error $\|G_\phi - G^*\|$ has a known convergence rate that depends on the smoothness and compositional structure of the quantile function, not on the ambient dimension of the data. Specifically, if the conditional quantile function has compositional structure with effective dimension $k$ at each layer and smoothness $\beta$, the mean integrated squared error converges at rate $O(N^{-2\beta/(2\beta+k+1)})$ where $N$ is the number of training pairs. This is the minimax rate for nonparametric estimation in $k+1$ dimensions (the extra 1 comes from the quantile level $\tau$), regardless of the dimension of $z$. We develop these theoretical guarantees in @sec-proofs.




## The IQN Architecture: A Preview {#sec-intro-iqn-preview}

The computational engine of GBC is the **Implicit Quantile Network** (IQN), introduced by @dabney2018implicit in the context of distributional reinforcement learning. The IQN was originally designed to learn the distribution of future rewards in an RL agent playing Atari games. We repurpose it for statistical inference, learning the distribution of parameters given data --- the posterior. We give a brief preview here; full details are in @sec-iqn.

An IQN takes two inputs: a covariate vector $x$ (or summary statistic $z$) and a quantile level $\tau \in (0,1)$. It outputs an estimate of the $\tau$th conditional quantile:
$$
\hat{Q}(\tau \mid x) \approx F^{-1}_{Y \mid X=x}(\tau).
$$ {#eq-intro-iqn-basic}

What makes the IQN "implicit" is that $\tau$ is treated as a continuous input, not a fixed grid. During training, $\tau$ values are sampled uniformly from $(0,1)$, so the network learns the *entire* quantile function simultaneously. This is a departure from classical quantile regression, which fits a separate model for each quantile level. If you want the median and a 95% interval using classical quantile regression, you fit three separate models (at $\tau = 0.025, 0.5, 0.975$). With an IQN, you train a single model and evaluate it at any $\tau$ you like.

This has a subtle but important consequence: the IQN encourages *monotonicity* of the quantile function in $\tau$ through soft constraints in the loss, whereas fitting separate quantile regression models offers no guarantee that $\hat{Q}(\tau_1 \mid x) \leq \hat{Q}(\tau_2 \mid x)$ for $\tau_1 < \tau_2$. Quantile crossing is a well-known problem in classical quantile regression, and the IQN's implicit treatment of $\tau$ largely resolves it.

The architecture has three components:

1. *Cosine embedding.* The scalar $\tau \in (0,1)$ is lifted into a high-dimensional representation using a cosine basis:
$$
\varphi(\tau) = \big(\cos(\pi \tau \cdot 1), \; \cos(\pi \tau \cdot 2), \; \ldots, \; \cos(\pi \tau \cdot M)\big).
$$
This gives the network a rich representation of the quantile level. The cosine functions form an orthogonal basis on $[0,1]$, so different $\tau$ values produce linearly independent embeddings. This is analogous to positional encoding in transformers: a scalar (position or quantile level) is mapped to a high-dimensional vector that the network can process more effectively than a raw scalar input. In our experiments, $M = 64$ cosine basis functions work well for most problems.

2. *Feature extraction.* The input $x$ (or summary statistic $z = S(y)$) is processed by a standard MLP --- typically 2--3 hidden layers with ReLU activations --- to produce a feature vector $f(x) \in \mathbb{R}^M$ of the same dimension as the cosine embedding.

3. *Elementwise combination.* The features and the quantile embedding are combined via elementwise (Hadamard) multiplication:
$$
h = f(x) \odot \varphi(\tau),
$$
then passed through one or more output layers to produce $\hat{Q}(\tau \mid x) \in \mathbb{R}$. The elementwise multiplication creates interactions between the covariate features and the quantile level, allowing the network to learn how the shape of the conditional distribution varies with $x$. Homoscedastic data (constant variance) produces feature vectors that are nearly independent of $x$; heteroscedastic data produces feature vectors that modulate the quantile embedding differently at different $x$ values.

The elementwise multiplication is the central architectural choice. Alternative combination strategies --- concatenation, addition, attention --- have been explored in the distributional RL literature, but multiplication has a natural interpretation: it creates a *multiplicative interaction* between what the network knows about the input ($f(x)$) and what it knows about the quantile level ($\varphi(\tau)$). When the conditional distribution is homoscedastic, the quantile function has the form $Q(\tau \mid x) = \mu(x) + \sigma \cdot \Phi^{-1}(\tau)$, and the multiplicative architecture can represent this by making $f(x)$ encode the mean and $\varphi(\tau)$ encode the quantile offset.

*Training* uses the pinball loss (also called the check loss or asymmetric absolute loss):
$$
\rho_\tau(u) = u \cdot (\tau - \mathbf{1}_{u < 0}) = \max(\tau u, \; (\tau - 1)u).
$$ {#eq-intro-pinball}

For each training sample $(x_i, y_i)$ and a randomly drawn $\tau$, the loss penalizes under-prediction at rate $\tau$ and over-prediction at rate $1 - \tau$. When $\tau = 0.9$, for example, under-predicting is penalized nine times more heavily than over-predicting, which pushes the prediction toward the 90th percentile. When $\tau = 0.1$, the asymmetry reverses. Minimizing the expected pinball loss yields the true conditional quantile --- this is a classical result from @koenker1978regression, extended here from linear models to deep networks.

In practice, the raw pinball loss alone can produce quantile functions that are noisy or that cross at certain covariate values. We therefore use a *three-term composite loss* that adds a location anchor (penalizing deviation from the conditional mean, which stabilizes training) and a soft non-crossing penalty (penalizing $Q(\tau_1 \mid x) > Q(\tau_2 \mid x)$ for $\tau_1 < \tau_2$, which enforces monotonicity) to the pinball term. The default weights are $(0.3, 0.3, 0.4)$ for the three components. The details are developed in @sec-iqn-loss.




## Five Things GBC Does {#sec-intro-five-applications}

The same IQN architecture and training procedure apply across five application domains. We describe each in enough detail to convey why simulation-based methods are essential and what specific inferential questions GBC answers. Later chapters develop each application in full. In every case, the posterior or predictive distribution is learned as a quantile function from simulated data, and inference is a forward pass through a trained network.

*Surrogates for computer experiments.*
Computer simulators --- finite element codes, climate models, aerodynamic solvers --- are expensive to run. A single evaluation of a CFD code for the NASA LGBB rocket takes hours on a high-performance cluster. A full uncertainty quantification study might require tens of thousands of evaluations, which is simply infeasible at the original fidelity. A *surrogate* is a fast statistical approximation that can stand in for the simulator, providing predictions and uncertainty estimates at a fraction of the computational cost. The traditional tool is the Gaussian process (GP), which provides a posterior predictive distribution over the simulator output [@rasmussen2006gaussian; @santner2018design; @gramacy2020surrogates]. GPs are exact interpolators with well-calibrated uncertainty bands and have served the computer experiments community well for decades.

But GPs have well-known scaling limitations. The $O(n^3)$ cost of inverting the covariance matrix makes them infeasible for large datasets: a GP with $n = 5{,}000$ training points requires factoring a $5{,}000 \times 5{,}000$ matrix, which takes minutes; at $n = 20{,}000$ it becomes impractical, and at $n = 90{,}000$ it is out of the question. The Gaussian predictive distribution is also restrictive for heteroscedastic or multimodal outputs, and the stationarity assumption breaks down at discontinuities. GBC replaces the GP with an IQN trained on simulator input-output pairs. The cost is $O(NLw^2)$, scaling linearly in the number of training points. The predictive distribution is arbitrary --- no Gaussianity assumed, no stationarity required. Engineers who previously waited hours for a GP fit on a few hundred carefully chosen design points can now train an IQN on tens of thousands of simulator runs and obtain a richer predictive distribution that captures heteroscedasticity and non-Gaussianity automatically.

In our empirical evaluation on the BGP benchmark suite --- a standard collection of piecewise smooth test functions with jump discontinuities --- GBC improves CRPS (continuous ranked probability score, the gold standard metric for probabilistic prediction) by 11--46% over GP and mixed jump GP baselines. The improvement is largest on surfaces with sharp discontinuities, where the GP's stationarity assumption causes it to smooth across boundaries, while the IQN learns the discontinuity location and produces sharp, well-calibrated predictive distributions on both sides. GBC scales comfortably to $n = 90{,}000$ training points where dense-covariance GPs are infeasible due to the $O(n^3)$ matrix inversion cost. For smooth surfaces in low dimensions ($n < 2{,}000$, $d \leq 4$), GPs retain a slight edge because their strong inductive bias (stationarity, smoothness) is correct for these problems. But GBC is competitive even there, and far more scalable. The details are in @sec-surrogates and @sec-jumps, where we develop the Aug-IQN architecture --- an augmented IQN with boundary detection --- for response surfaces with sharp discontinuities.

*Bayesian inference.* The goal is to learn the posterior $\pi(\theta \mid y)$ from simulated (parameter, data) pairs, turning Bayesian inference into a supervised learning problem. The framework is quite general: it handles both parametric models where the likelihood can be written down but is expensive to evaluate, and simulator-based models where no likelihood exists at all. The key requirement is the ability to simulate from the forward model --- draw parameter values from the prior and generate corresponding data.

GBC then learns the map from data summaries to posterior quantiles, producing an amortized inference engine that works for any future observed dataset. The learned map $G_\phi(\tau, z)$ is a deterministic function that takes a quantile level $\tau \in (0,1)$ and a data summary $z = S(y)$ and returns the corresponding posterior quantile. Drawing $\tau$ uniformly produces posterior samples; evaluating at $\tau = 0.5$ gives the posterior median; evaluating at $\tau = 0.025$ and $\tau = 0.975$ gives a 95% credible interval. All of these are forward passes through the same trained network.

We calibrate GBC on the normal-normal conjugate model (where the analytic posterior is known, as in @sec-intro-normal-normal) and on a bimodal posterior (where MCMC must be run carefully to avoid missing modes). Both examples confirm that GBC recovers the correct posterior.

The bimodal case is instructive. When the posterior has two well-separated modes, a random-walk Metropolis chain can get trapped in one mode for very long periods, producing a biased sample that misrepresents the posterior. Running multiple chains from different starting points helps, but requires careful initialization and monitoring. The trained IQN, by contrast, captures both modes automatically: the quantile function maps different $\tau$ values to different modes. Low $\tau$ values (near 0) map to the lower mode, high $\tau$ values (near 1) map to the upper mode, and intermediate $\tau$ values capture the valley between them. This is a consequence of the quantile function's monotonicity: it must pass through both modes on its way from $-\infty$ to $+\infty$, so it cannot miss either one. The full development is in @sec-bayesian-inference.

*Prediction.*
Given observations $Z_{1:n} = (X_1, Y_1), \ldots, (X_n, Y_n)$, predict the next outcome $Y_{n+1}$ at covariates $x_{n+1}$. This is arguably the most common task in applied statistics, and the Bayesian approach handles it naturally through the posterior predictive distribution $p(y_{n+1} \mid x_{n+1}, Z_{1:n}) = \int p(y_{n+1} \mid x_{n+1}, \theta) \, \pi(\theta \mid Z_{1:n}) \, d\theta$. The integral marginalizes over parameter uncertainty, giving predictions that account for both the noise in the data and the uncertainty about the model.

GBC learns the predictive quantile function directly:
$$
Y_{n+1} = Q(\tau, x_{n+1}, S(Z_{1:n})), \quad \tau \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1),
$$
bypassing explicit computation of the prior, the likelihood, and the integral. The summary statistic $S(Z_{1:n})$ compresses the training data into a fixed-dimensional vector that captures the relevant information for prediction. For example, in a regression problem, $S$ might include the coefficients of a fitted model, sample moments, or features learned by a neural network.

The de Finetti--Ressel representation theorem provides the theoretical justification for this approach. It guarantees that for exchangeable data, there exists an implicit prior and likelihood such that the predictive distribution $P(Y_{n+1} \mid Z_{1:n})$ is a proper Bayesian predictive. The quantile transport map $Q(\tau, x, S)$ represents this predictive distribution without ever specifying the prior or likelihood explicitly. This is a subtle but important point: the Bayesian validity comes from the exchangeability assumption and the representation theorem, not from a specific choice of prior.

The "parameter" we are learning about is the next observation $Y_{n+1}$ itself --- not a fixed unknown quantity, but a future random variable. This reframing collapses the distinction between parameter inference and predictive inference into a single computational framework. In both cases, we learn a conditional quantile function from simulated data; the only difference is whether the target variable is a parameter $\theta$ or a future observation $Y_{n+1}$.

The predictive quantile function directly gives prediction intervals: for any coverage level $1 - \alpha$, the interval $[Q(\alpha/2, x_{n+1}, S(Z_{1:n})), \; Q(1 - \alpha/2, x_{n+1}, S(Z_{1:n}))]$ is an approximate $(1-\alpha)$ prediction interval. Unlike conformal prediction intervals, which guarantee only *marginal* coverage (averaged over the randomness in $X_{n+1}$), the GBC prediction intervals aim for *conditional* coverage (valid for each specific $x_{n+1}$). We show in @sec-prediction that these intervals have better coverage and shorter width than conformal prediction intervals in settings where the data have compositional structure that deep networks can exploit, while conformal prediction retains advantages when the model is misspecified (since conformal guarantees hold without any modeling assumptions).

*Maximum expected utility.*
Decision theory is the natural companion to Bayesian inference. Having computed the posterior distribution $\pi(\theta \mid y_{\text{obs}})$, we want to use it to make optimal decisions. The foundational principle: choose the action $a$ that maximizes expected utility $E[U(a, Y) \mid y_{\text{obs}}]$, where the expectation is over the posterior predictive distribution of future outcomes $Y$. This principle, due to @savage1954foundations, provides a complete framework for rational decision-making under uncertainty.

The classical approach to computing expected utility requires integrating the utility function $U(a, y)$ over the posterior predictive distribution $p(y \mid y_{\text{obs}}) = \int p(y \mid \theta) \pi(\theta \mid y_{\text{obs}}) \, d\theta$ --- a double integral (over parameters and outcomes) that is often intractable. Even when the posterior is available via MCMC, computing expected utility requires an additional layer of Monte Carlo integration that introduces variance and computational cost. For each candidate action $a$, you need to draw posterior samples $\theta^{(1)}, \ldots, \theta^{(T)}$, then for each $\theta^{(t)}$ simulate a future outcome $y^{(t)} \sim p(y \mid \theta^{(t)})$, and finally average $U(a, y^{(t)})$ over $t$. This nested Monte Carlo procedure can be slow and noisy.

GBC sidesteps this via a *quantile identity* for expected utility. For any random variable $X$ with quantile function $Q_X(\tau) = F_X^{-1}(\tau)$, the expected value can be written as:
$$
E[X] = \int_0^1 Q_X(\tau) \, d\tau.
$$ {#eq-intro-quantile-identity}
This is simply the statement that the mean of a distribution equals the average of its quantile function over the unit interval. Applying this to $U(X)$ gives:
$$
E[U(X)] = \int_0^1 Q_{U(X)}(\tau) \, d\tau,
$$
where $Q_{U(X)}$ is the quantile function of the random variable $U(X)$. For monotone utility $U$, the compositional identity gives $Q_{U(X)}(\tau) = U(Q_X(\tau))$. (This identity holds when $U$ is monotone; for general utility functions, the expected utility integral must be evaluated differently, as $Q_{U(X)}(\tau) \neq U(Q_X(\tau))$ when $U$ is non-monotone.) Since IQN directly produces quantile functions, expected utility is just a one-dimensional integral over $\tau$ --- no density estimation, no posterior sampling, no nested Monte Carlo. The integral is computed by simple numerical quadrature (trapezoidal rule or Gauss-Legendre) over the unit interval, evaluating the IQN at a grid of $\tau$ values and averaging.

This reflects a connection between quantile-based inference and decision theory that traces back to Yaari's dual theory of choice under risk [@yaari1987dual]. In Yaari's framework, preferences are defined over cumulative distributions rather than outcomes, and the evaluation functional is linear in probabilities rather than in utilities. Wang's distortion operator [@wang2000class] formalizes the Bayesian updating step in this quantile framework: the posterior quantile function is obtained by composing the prior quantile function with a learned distortion, exactly the operation that the IQN performs. We develop these connections and their computational implications in @sec-meu, including portfolio optimization under model uncertainty.

*Causal inference.*
Estimating treatment effects from observational data requires controlling for confounders. The fundamental problem is that we never observe both potential outcomes --- $Y(1)$ under treatment and $Y(0)$ under control --- for the same individual. This is the "fundamental problem of causal inference" [@holland1986statistics], and it means that every causal estimator must make assumptions about the relationship between observed and missing outcomes.

Under the assumption of unconfoundedness (no unmeasured confounders, formalized as $Y(0), Y(1) \perp\!\!\!\perp Z \mid X$ where $Z$ is the treatment indicator), the conditional average treatment effect $\tau(x) = E[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid X = x]$ can be identified from observational data. But estimating it well requires simultaneously solving three sub-problems: learning the propensity score $e(x) = P(Z = 1 \mid X = x)$ (who gets treated), learning the conditional outcome distribution $P(Y \mid X, Z)$ (what outcomes look like), and combining them to estimate the heterogeneous treatment effect $\tau(x)$.

GBC extends naturally to this setting via a three-part loss that jointly estimates all three quantities. The propensity component (a binary cross-entropy loss) ensures that the model learns which covariates predict treatment assignment; the quantile component (the pinball loss applied to observed outcomes) learns the full conditional distribution of outcomes; and the treatment-effect component (an MSE loss applied to the treatment effect estimate) regularizes the CATE estimate. The three losses are weighted and summed, and the entire model is trained end-to-end by stochastic gradient descent.

The resulting estimator integrates treatment effect estimation over the full conditional distribution --- not just the conditional mean --- which provides richer information about treatment heterogeneity. Because the IQN produces the entire conditional quantile function of outcomes, we can compute not just the average treatment effect but quantile-specific treatment effects: how does the treatment affect the 10th percentile of outcomes? The 90th percentile? These quantile treatment effects (QTEs) reveal aspects of treatment heterogeneity that the conditional mean alone cannot capture. For instance, a treatment might have no effect on average but a large positive effect on the worst outcomes, a pattern that is invisible to mean-based estimators but immediately apparent from the quantile treatment effects.

On the LaLonde job-training benchmark, GBC detects that individuals in the top quartile of predicted benefit gain roughly three times more from the program than those in the bottom quartile, a finding that both double machine learning (DML) and Bayesian causal forests (BCF) corroborate but with less precision.

When the confounding structure is low-dimensional ($k \ll p$), GBC achieves a minimax rate of $O(n^{-2\beta/(2\beta+k)})$ compared to DML's $O(n^{-2\beta/(2\beta+p)})$, because the IQN exploits compositional structure that linear methods cannot. For instance, with smoothness $\beta = 2$, $p = 20$ covariates, and effective confounding dimension $k = 3$, the GBC rate is $O(n^{-4/7})$ versus DML's $O(n^{-1/6})$ --- a substantial difference in finite samples. At $n = 1{,}000$, this means GBC's estimation error is roughly $1{,}000^{-4/7} \approx 0.019$ while DML's is $1{,}000^{-1/6} \approx 0.32$, a factor of 25 difference. The source of this advantage is that GBC's deep network architecture exploits the compositional structure of the confounding mechanism, effectively reducing the problem from $p = 20$ dimensions to $k = 3$ dimensions, while DML's linear first stage operates in the full $p$-dimensional space. See @sec-causal for the full development.




## GBC versus Classical Bayesian Computation {#sec-intro-vs-classical}

How does this book relate to the classical Bayesian computational toolbox --- MCMC, variational inference, expectation propagation, and Gaussian process emulation [see, e.g., @gelman2013bayesian; @robert2004monte; @brooks2011handbook]? The relationship is complementary, not adversarial. Classical methods and GBC share the same inferential goals --- posterior distributions, predictive distributions, and decision analysis --- but they differ in their computational strategy. A reader who has learned Bayesian modeling through the MCMC workflow will find that GBC provides a different computational route to the same destination. A reader who encounters GBC first will find that classical texts provide essential background on model building, prior specification, and model checking that this book does not attempt to replace.

The two approaches also differ in their scope of applicability. Classical Bayesian computation shines when the model is explicit --- when you can write down $p(y \mid \theta)$ and $\pi(\theta)$ and compute the posterior via MCMC or analytical approximation. The standard workflow is well-established: specify the model, code it in Stan or PyMC, run MCMC, check convergence, interpret the posterior. This workflow has been refined over decades and is supported by excellent diagnostics and visualization tools.

GBC shines when the model is implicit --- when you have a forward simulator but no closed-form likelihood. The GBC workflow is different: specify the prior, write a simulator, generate training pairs, train an IQN, and then query the trained network for any observed dataset. This workflow is newer and less mature, but it applies to a strictly larger class of models.

In the overlap region where both approaches apply --- models with explicit likelihoods and moderate dimension --- they should give the same answers. We verify this explicitly in @sec-bayesian-inference on the normal-normal conjugate model and a bimodal posterior. The choice between them is then a matter of computational efficiency and workflow: MCMC for single-dataset analyses where convergence is fast, GBC for multi-dataset deployments where amortization pays off.

@tbl-intro-classical maps the correspondence between standard Bayesian methods and their GBC counterparts.

| *Classical Approach* | *GBC Alternative* | *Where in This Book* |
|---|---|---|
| MCMC | IQN trained by SGD --- no chains | @sec-iqn, @sec-bayesian-inference |
| Variational inference / EP | GBC is exact (quantile transport) | @sec-noise-outsourcing, @sec-bayesian-inference |
| GP regression | IQN surrogates --- $O(n)$ not $O(n^3)$ | @sec-surrogates, @sec-jumps |
| Mixture models | Aug-IQN with EM + classifier | @sec-jumps |
| Decision analysis | MEU via quantile identity --- density-free | @sec-meu |
| Posterior predictive checks | Generative prediction via quantile transport | @sec-prediction |

: Correspondence between classical Bayesian methods and GBC. Each standard method has a GBC counterpart that achieves the same inferential target via different computation. {#tbl-intro-classical}

The philosophical difference is in what each approach assumes:

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" title="Classical Bayes vs GBC: What You Need"}
*Classical Bayesian computation* assumes you can *write down* the likelihood $p(y \mid \theta)$ and *evaluate* it pointwise. This is essential for MCMC, which proposes parameter values and accepts or rejects based on the likelihood ratio.

*GBC* assumes you can *simulate* from the likelihood. You need a forward model that generates synthetic data given parameters, but you never need to evaluate $p(y \mid \theta)$ as a function. Simulation is strictly weaker than evaluation --- and it is often all you have.
:::

When should you use MCMC, and when should you use GBC?

*MCMC is better when* the model is low-dimensional (say $d \leq 5$) with a well-behaved posterior that allows the chain to converge quickly. MCMC is also preferred when you need detailed posterior diagnostics such as effective sample size and divergent transitions, which provide information about model pathologies that GBC does not directly offer. If you have a single dataset with no need for amortization and a closed-form likelihood, MCMC lets you exploit conjugacy or gradient information via HMC, and the cost of running a single chain is modest.

*GBC is better when* the likelihood has no closed form --- as in simulator-based and agent-based models --- or when you need amortized inference across many datasets such as production deployments or sensor networks. If a research lab needs to fit the same model to data from 5,000 sensors, MCMC requires 5,000 separate chain runs (at 30 seconds each, that is over 40 hours), while GBC trains once (say, 2 hours) and then runs 5,000 forward passes in about 4 minutes total. GBC is also the right choice when the model involves high-dimensional data that demands linear scaling, when you want the full predictive quantile function rather than just posterior samples, or when decision-making requires computing expected utilities, which are naturally expressed through quantile functions.

There is no universal winner. We want to be clear about what GBC is *not*. It is not a replacement for careful model building --- you still need to choose the right prior and the right simulator. It is not a black box that eliminates the need for statistical thinking --- you still need to choose summary statistics, check calibration, and validate your results. And it is not a magic bullet for high-dimensional parameter spaces --- while GBC scales linearly in the number of training points, the number of training points needed for accurate posterior estimation grows with the dimension of $\theta$, just as it does for any nonparametric method.

What GBC *is* is a computational framework that replaces MCMC's Markov chain with a trained neural network, ABC's local kernel with a global quantile function, and variational inference's parametric family with a nonparametric quantile representation.

The contribution of this book is fourfold.
First, we develop the theoretical foundations of GBC, connecting the noise outsourcing theorem,
Parzen's quantile framework, and deep network approximation theory into a rigorous
mathematical framework.
Second, we provide the IQN architecture and training procedures, implemented in the
open-source `gbc` Python package (<https://github.com/VadimSokolov/gbc>),
that make GBC practical.
Third, we demonstrate GBC across five application domains --- surrogates, inference,
prediction, decision-making, and causal inference --- showing that it is competitive with
or superior to existing methods in each.
Fourth, we are honest about GBC's limitations, documenting the failure modes and
developing remedies (heteroscedastic ensembles, conformal calibration)
that extend GBC's applicability.




## Historical Note {#sec-intro-history}

The ideas behind GBC have roots in several distinct intellectual traditions. Tracing these lineages helps explain why the framework arrived when it did and not earlier.

The story begins with Emanuel Parzen, who argued throughout his career that quantile functions --- not densities --- are the natural language of statistics. In his influential 1979 paper on nonparametric statistical data modeling and in his later work [@parzen2004quantile], Parzen developed what he called the "quantile approach" to statistics: every distributional question should be formulated in terms of the quantile function $Q(\tau) = F^{-1}(\tau)$, and every statistical operation should be expressed as a transformation of quantile functions. This was regarded by many as an aesthetic preference, but it turns out to be computationally fundamental.

The compositional identity $Q_{g(Y)}(\tau) = g(Q_Y(\tau))$ for monotone $g$ --- a simple consequence of Parzen's framework --- is precisely the property that connects quantile functions to deep learning, where function composition is the defining architectural principle. Parzen also introduced the "comparison distribution" $D(\tau, x)$ that decomposes conditional quantiles as $Q_{Y|X}(\tau \mid x) = Q_Y(D(\tau, x))$, an insight that anticipates Wang's distortion operator and, ultimately, the IQN's learned transport map. The comparison distribution tells us how conditioning on $X = x$ distorts the unconditional quantile function --- it is a learned warping of the probability scale, and it is the natural representation of Bayesian updating when you think in quantiles rather than densities. Around the same time, @koenker1978regression developed linear quantile regression, showing that the $\tau$th quantile of $Y \mid X$ can be estimated by minimizing the asymmetric absolute loss (the pinball loss). This gave Parzen's quantile philosophy a concrete computational method, one that we extend from linear models to deep networks throughout this book.

The second thread is Donald Rubin's 1984 paper "Bayesianly Justifiable and Relevant Frequency Calculations for the Applied Statistician" [@rubin1984bayesianly]. Rubin's contribution was to show that Bayesian inference can be understood as a simulation exercise: if you can simulate parameters from the prior and data from the likelihood, then the subset of simulations that match the observed data constitutes a sample from the posterior. Consider the joint distribution of $(\theta, y)$ where $\theta \sim \pi(\theta)$ and $y \mid \theta \sim p(y \mid \theta)$. The conditional distribution of $\theta$ given $y = y_{\text{obs}}$ is, by definition, the posterior $\pi(\theta \mid y_{\text{obs}})$. So if we simulate many pairs $(\theta_i, y_i)$ from the joint and keep only those where $y_i = y_{\text{obs}}$ (or $y_i \approx y_{\text{obs}}$), we obtain posterior samples.

This insight --- that *simulation is sufficient for Bayesian inference* --- is the foundational principle of both ABC and GBC. The difference is in how "matching" is defined: ABC uses a local kernel around the observed summary statistics, accepting $\theta_i$ when $\|S(y_i) - S(y_{\text{obs}})\| < \varepsilon$, while GBC learns a global quantile transport map that works for all possible observed datasets simultaneously. But the philosophical starting point is the same, and it is Rubin's. Rubin's paper was primarily about the interpretation of frequentist procedures in a Bayesian framework, and the computational implications were not its main focus. The computational exploitation of Rubin's insight had to wait for the development of ABC in the late 1990s [@tavare1997inferring; @beaumont2002approximate] and for GBC in the 2020s.

The third thread comes from a surprising direction: reinforcement learning. In 2017, Bellemare, Dabney, and Munos introduced C51 [@bellemare2017distributional], an algorithm that learns the *distribution* of future returns in an RL agent, not just the expected return. This was a departure from classical RL, where the value function $V(s) = E[\sum_t \gamma^t r_t \mid s]$ is a scalar. Distributional RL replaces $V(s)$ with a random variable $Z(s)$ whose distribution captures the full uncertainty about future outcomes. The motivation was practical --- risk-sensitive control requires knowing the full distribution of returns, not just the mean --- but the mathematical framework that emerged turned out to be broadly useful. @dabney2017distributional showed that the 1-Wasserstein distance between distributions is minimized by quantile regression, providing the theoretical link between distributional RL and quantile estimation.

The following year, @dabney2018implicit proposed the Implicit Quantile Network (IQN), which represents the return distribution via its quantile function and trains with the pinball loss. The IQN architecture --- cosine embedding of $\tau$, elementwise combination with state features, training via the check loss --- was designed for Atari games, but it is precisely the architecture that GBC needs for posterior quantile estimation. The connection is not accidental: both problems involve learning a conditional distribution (of returns given state, or of parameters given data) from simulated experience. An Atari agent simulates many game trajectories and learns the distribution of returns conditional on state; a Bayesian analyst simulates many (parameter, data) pairs and learns the posterior distribution conditional on data summaries. The mathematical structure is identical, and the IQN handles both.

The synthesis arrived in @polson2024generative, which recognized that these three threads --- Parzen's quantile philosophy, Rubin's simulation principle, and Dabney's IQN architecture --- could be woven into a unified computational framework for Bayesian inference. The noise outsourcing theorem [@kallenberg1997foundations] provides the theoretical guarantee that the conditional quantile function exists and is the right object to learn. The universal approximation theorem for deep ReLU networks [@schmidt-hieber2020nonparametric] guarantees that the IQN can learn it. And the pinball loss provides a proper scoring rule for training. The convergence rates depend on the effective dimensionality of the compositional structure, not the ambient dimension of the data, which is why GBC escapes the curse of dimensionality that plagues ABC's kernel estimators.

GBC is thus not a single invention but a convergence of ideas from statistics, probability, and machine learning --- each necessary, none sufficient alone. Parzen gave us the right mathematical objects (quantile functions). Rubin gave us the right computational principle (simulation is sufficient for Bayesian inference). Koenker gave us the right loss function (the pinball loss). Dabney gave us the right architecture (the IQN with cosine embedding). And Kallenberg gave us the right theorem (noise outsourcing). This book assembles these pieces into a coherent framework and develops the theory, algorithms, and applications that make it practical.

Why did this synthesis take so long? Each ingredient was available by 2018 at the latest (Kallenberg's theorem dates to 1997), yet the framework was not assembled until 2024. The reason, we believe, is disciplinary fragmentation: quantile statisticians were not reading the RL literature, RL researchers were not thinking about Bayesian inference, and Bayesian statisticians were invested in MCMC as the canonical computational tool. GBC required someone to see the connection between distributional RL and Bayesian posterior estimation --- both are conditional distribution learning problems --- and to recognize that Parzen's quantile philosophy provides the theoretical foundation that makes the connection precise. We hope this book helps bridge the disciplinary boundaries and makes the connections visible to a broader audience.




## Road Map {#sec-intro-roadmap}

The book has three parts, fourteen chapters, and two appendices. Here is how they fit together.

### Part I: Foundations (Chapters 1--5)

You are reading Chapter 1. The remaining four foundation chapters build the theoretical machinery piece by piece, each chapter introducing one essential component of the GBC framework.

In @sec-datasets, we introduce the datasets that serve as running examples throughout the book. Each dataset is chosen to illustrate a specific challenge that GBC addresses, and each appears in multiple chapters as the methods are developed.

The motorcycle crash data consists of 133 observations of head acceleration versus time after impact, originally from a helmet-testing experiment. The data exhibit a sharp transition from low variance (before impact) to high variance (during impact) to moderate variance (after impact), making it a canonical test for heteroscedastic models. The Phantom and Star surfaces are 2D response surfaces with sharp discontinuities --- piecewise smooth regions separated by curved boundaries where the response jumps abruptly --- that defeat GP surrogates relying on stationarity and smoothness. These benchmarks are drawn from the computer experiments literature and represent the kind of challenge that arises when simulating phase transitions, regime changes, or structural failures. The NASA LGBB rocket aerodynamics benchmark provides 300 design points in 3 dimensions (Mach number, angle of attack, sideslip angle) for predicting drag coefficient, a problem where GBC achieves $2.95\times$ lower RMSE than deep GPs. The lake temperature forecasting problem is a real-world calibration challenge where a physics-based simulator must be calibrated to observed temperature profiles, and GBC achieves RMSE of 1.219 with 90.2% coverage. The LaLonde causal inference dataset contains 445 observations from a randomized job-training program conducted in the 1970s, providing a benchmark where the true average treatment effect is known from the experimental design (approximately \$1,500--\$2,000 in 1978 dollars, or about 0.8--1.0 in log earnings). This dataset is the gold standard for evaluating causal inference methods because it provides a ground truth against which observational estimators can be validated. Each dataset is loaded, explored, and visualized so that the reader has a concrete reference point before the methods are developed.

In @sec-quantiles, we develop Parzen's framework for quantile-based statistics from first principles. We start with the basics --- the quantile function $Q(\tau) = F^{-1}(\tau) = \inf\{x : F(x) \geq \tau\}$, its relationship to the CDF $F$, and fundamental properties like the probability integral transform ($F(X) \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)$ for continuous $F$) and the inverse transform ($Q(U) \sim F$ for $U \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)$). We then introduce the check loss (pinball loss) $\rho_\tau(u) = u(\tau - \mathbf{1}_{u<0})$ and prove the classical result that minimizing the expected pinball loss yields the conditional $\tau$th quantile. We cover linear quantile regression [@koenker1978regression], which extends ordinary least squares from the conditional mean to the conditional $\tau$th quantile by replacing the squared loss with the pinball loss, and discuss subgradient methods for optimization (the pinball loss is not differentiable at zero, requiring subgradient or interior-point methods).
